text: The Great Rift Valley is a giant [[@valleys|system of valleys]] where the [[@earth-layers-crust|Earth's crust]] is being slowly pulled apart. It runs from the Red Sea down through Ethiopia, Kenya and Tanzania towards Mozambique. Along the way are steep cliffs, deep lakes and volcanoes.

Beneath it, hot rock rising from the [[mantle|mantle]] is stretching the crust like dough. As the crust thins, long strips of land drop down between cracks called faults, making the valley floor. East Africa is splitting away from the rest of the continent at a few millimetres a year.
The name was given in the 1890s by the British [[geologist|geologist]] John Walter Gregory, who explored the valley in Kenya. Today, scientists also call the African part the East African Rift.

st.prompt: If the Great Rift Valley keeps pulling apart for millions of years, what will most likely happen?

options.t: The sea will flood in and a new ocean will form
It will close up again and form tall mountains
Nothing, because rift valleys stop moving

st.reveal: The Red Sea is an example of what comes next. It began as a rift on land, and when the gap grew wide and low enough, sea water poured in. Geologists expect parts of East Africa to follow, though it will take millions of years.

d.try: Roll out a slab of play dough or soft clay on a table and hold both ends. Pull them apart slowly. Watch where the middle thins, sags and cracks. That sagging middle is a model of a rift valley.
myth: Africa will split in two any day now, because of a giant crack that opened in Kenya in 2018.
That crack was real, but scientists think it was mostly made by heavy rain washing out soft volcanic ash. The rift itself moves only millimetres a year, and a new ocean is millions of years away.

sec.h: A continent tearing in slow motion
sec.t:
Africa sits on a [[plate|plate]] that is slowly breaking into two. The larger part is called the Nubian plate and the eastern part the Somali plate. The [[@continental-drift|continents drift]] all the time, but here you can watch the very start of a split, before any ocean has formed.

The Afar region of Ethiopia is where it is happening fastest. In 2005, the ground there cracked open along about 60 km, in roughly ten days. In places the gap was several metres wide. Scientists rushed in with satellites and instruments to measure it. Further north, the rift has already flooded. The Red Sea itself is a rift that the ocean poured into millions of years ago.

When land drops in a rift, water fills the low places. Lake Tanganyika is about 1,470 m deep, the second-deepest lake on Earth. Lake Malawi and Lake Turkana are rift lakes too.

Some rift lakes, like Lake Natron in Tanzania, are so salty and full of soda that few animals can live in them. Yet huge flocks of lesser [[@flamingos-pink|flamingos]] breed there, feeding on the tiny [[algae|algae]] that thrive in that harsh water.

Where the crust is thin, [[magma|magma]] pushes up. Mount [[@kilimanjaro|Kilimanjaro]] and Mount Kenya were built by this rift activity. Ol Doinyo Lengai in Tanzania erupts a rare [[lava|lava]] that is black when it comes out and cools to white, unlike any other active [[@volcano|volcano]] on Earth.

{{story:human-evolution}}

Some of the most important [[fossil|fossils]] of early humans and their relatives have been found in the rift. In 1974, scientists at Hadar in Ethiopia found much of a skeleton about 3.2 million years old. They nicknamed her Lucy. She walked upright but had a small brain, closer in size to a chimpanzee's.

At Olduvai Gorge in Tanzania, Mary and Louis Leakey and their team found [[@stone-tools|stone tools]] and fossils almost 2 million years old. They changed ideas about when our ancestors began making tools, a big chapter in the story of [[@human-evolution|human evolution]].

Why are there so many fossils here? Rifts sink and fill with layers of mud and volcanic ash, which bury bones quickly. Later, faults and erosion lift those layers back up where people can find them. The ash can also be dated, so scientists know how old the bones are.

If the stretching continues, the Somali plate will keep drifting east. Over millions of years the valley floor will sink lower, until the sea breaks in. Geologists think a new ocean could one day separate the Horn of Africa from the rest of the continent, giving East Africa a brand new coastline.

text: Sunlight is a mix of all colours. When it hits the tiny gas particles in air, blue light gets bounced around much more than red.
So blue light comes at you from all over the sky. That's why the sky looks blue.
At sunset, light travels through much more air. Most of the blue is bounced away, so red and orange reach you.

quiz.prompt: On the Moon, what colour is the sky in the middle of the day?

options.t: Black
Blue, like on Earth
Orange

quiz.reveal: Black. The Moon has almost no air, so there is nothing to scatter sunlight around the sky. Astronauts on the Moon saw a blazing Sun in a black sky, with Earth hanging overhead.

Now look through the glass straight at the torch. The light looks yellow-orange. The milk specks scatter blue light sideways, just as air does at sunset.
myth: The sky is blue because it reflects the ocean.

It's the other way round, mostly. Air scatters blue sunlight, which makes the sky blue even over deserts. The sea looks blue partly because it reflects the sky, and partly because water itself soaks up red light, which is what Raman showed.

sec.t:
In 1666, the young English scientist Isaac Newton passed sunlight through a glass [[prism|prism]] and split it into a band of colours, from red through to violet. Then he used a second prism to mix them back into white. White light, he showed, is all the colours together.

Each colour is light with a different [[wavelength|wavelength]]. Red has long waves, and blue and violet have short ones. That difference is the key to the blue sky. It's also why raindrops can spread sunlight into a [[@rainbow-how|rainbow]].

Air is mostly nitrogen and oxygen [[molecule|molecules]], far smaller than the wavelength of light. When sunlight hits them, some of it gets scattered in every direction. Short waves get scattered much more than long ones. In the 1870s, the British scientist Lord Rayleigh worked out the rule. Blue light is scattered about five times more strongly than red.

So as sunlight crosses the sky, blue light is thrown around everywhere. Wherever you look, away from [[@sun-what|the Sun]], some of that scattered blue is heading towards your eyes.

The same effect makes faraway hills look hazy and bluish, because there is so much air between you and them. Painters copy this to make their landscapes look deep, a trick called aerial [[@perspective|perspective]]. Climb higher, and there is less air above you to scatter light. That's why the sky looks a darker, deeper blue from a high mountain or an aeroplane window.
Violet light scatters even more than blue. But sunlight has less violet in it, some is absorbed high in the air, and our eyes are more sensitive to blue. So we see blue.

Cloud droplets are much bigger than air molecules. They scatter all colours about equally, so clouds look white or grey. [[@clouds-rain|How clouds form]].

At sunrise and sunset, sunlight takes a long, slanting path through the air. Most of the blue is scattered out along the way, leaving reds and oranges. Dust and smoke can make sunsets even redder. After the volcano Krakatoa erupted in Indonesia in 1883, its fine ash made skies glow red around the world for months.

On [[@mars-sky|Mars]], it's the opposite. Fine red dust in its thin air makes the daytime sky look butterscotch, and its sunsets look blue.

{{story:mars-sky}}

Raman studied how light changes colour slightly when it scatters off molecules. The ‘Raman effect’ is now used to identify chemicals, even in [[@art-detective|old paintings]].

In 1921, sailing to Europe, Raman looked at the deep blue Mediterranean and doubted the usual explanation that the sea just reflects the sky. Back in Calcutta, he and his student K.S. Krishnan studied how light scatters in liquids. On 28 February 1928, they announced that a tiny part of scattered light changes colour. India now celebrates that date as National Science Day. In 1930, Raman became the first Asian to win a Nobel Prize in science.

text: A planetarium is a theatre with a curved, dome-shaped ceiling that becomes a screen for the night sky. When the lights go down, a projector in the middle, or several around the edge, fills the dome with stars, planets and the [[@milky-way|Milky Way]].

The audience sits in reclining seats and looks up. The projector can copy the sky from any place on Earth, on any date, past or future. It can speed up time so you watch a whole night pass in a minute, or show where the planets will be next year.
Modern planetariums can also fly you through space, past the rings of Saturn or out to distant [[galaxy|galaxies]], using digital projectors that cover the whole dome.

st.prompt: In a planetarium, the operator can show you the sky over the North Pole, then over Antarctica, in a few seconds. How?

options.t: The projector tilts and turns to copy the view from anywhere on Earth
Cameras show live pictures from telescopes around the world
The dome itself spins and moves

st.reveal: A planetarium projector can be turned to match any place and any date. Tilt it one way and the North Star sits overhead, as at the North Pole. Tilt it the other way and the Southern Cross appears, as seen from Australia or Antarctica.

d.try: Make a mini planetarium. Ask an adult to help you poke small holes in the bottom of a paper cup in the shape of a constellation, like Orion. In a dark room, shine a phone torch into the cup and point it at the ceiling to project your stars.
myth: A planetarium and an observatory are the same thing.
An observatory has real telescopes for looking at the sky. A planetarium shows a projected sky on a dome indoors, so it works in daytime, in cloudy weather and in cities full of light.

sec.h: The machine that copies the sky
sec.t:
Before planetariums, people built mechanical models of the [[solar-system|solar system]], with balls on rods that turned with [[@antikythera|gears]], called orreries. But they showed the planets from outside, not the sky as we see it.

In the early 1920s, engineers at the Zeiss optics company in Germany, led by Walther Bauersfeld, came up with a new idea. They built a projector shaped a bit like a giant dumbbell, packed with lenses. Bright lamps inside shone through tiny holes to throw sharp points of light onto a dome.

It was tested in 1923 on the factory roof in Jena. A permanent planetarium opened at the Deutsches Museum in Munich soon after. Crowds queued to see it, and other cities soon wanted planetariums of their own.

A planetarium works because your brain is easy to fool. The dome is only a few metres above you, but because it curves all around and you can't see its edges in the dark, it feels like an endless sky. That is the same kind of brain trick behind many [[@optical-illusions|optical illusions]].

Many domes are made of thin metal sheets full of tiny holes. Speakers hidden behind the dome send sound through them, so music and voices seem to come from the sky. The room is kept very dark so your eyes can adjust and pick up faint stars, just as they would outdoors.

Many children in big cities have never seen the Milky Way, because streetlights and buildings drown out the faint stars. On a really dark night in the countryside, you might see a few thousand stars at once. A planetarium can show all of them, plus the stars only visible from the other side of the world.

That is why planetariums are popular with schools. Students learn to spot [[@constellations|constellations]], see how the Moon's shape changes and find out why the stars seem to wheel around the [[@north-star|North Star]]. Some then go outside to try [[@stargazing|stargazing]] for real.

text: The Konark Sun Temple, on the coast of [[@odisha|Odisha]], was built around 1250 CE for Surya, the Hindu Sun god. In Hindu stories, Surya rides across the sky every day in a [[@wheel-to-chariot|chariot]] pulled by seven [[@horses|horses]]. So the temple was designed as that chariot, made of stone.

Around its base are 24 huge carved wheels, 12 on each side. In front, stone horses strain forward as if pulling the whole temple towards the sunrise. The chariot shape was a way of turning a building into a story: the Sun's daily journey, frozen in stone.

st.prompt: The temple has 24 wheels. What do many people believe the 24 wheels stand for?

options.t: Divisions of time, such as months, fortnights or hours
The 24 kings who ruled Odisha before
The 24 villages that paid for the temple

st.reveal: There are 12 pairs of wheels. A common explanation is that they stand for the 12 months, or for the 24 fortnights in a year, or for the 24 hours of the day. All link the chariot to the Sun, which measures out time.

n.certNote: The temple's date, builder and chariot design are well established. Why the main tower fell, and how exactly the wheels were meant to work as sundials, are still debated.

d.try: On a sunny day, push a pencil upright into a lump of clay on a sheet of paper outdoors, in a safe spot near home. Mark where the pencil's shadow falls every hour and write the time beside it. You've made a simple sundial, like the ones people say the Konark wheels can work as.
myth: Konark's main tower fell because a giant magnet on top was removed.

This is a famous legend, said to explain why ships' compasses went wrong nearby. There is no evidence for a giant magnet. Historians think the tower fell because of weak foundations, sandy ground, storms or earthquakes, though nobody is sure which.

sec.t:
The temple was built by King Narasimhadeva I of the Eastern Ganga [[dynasty|dynasty]], who ruled much of what is now Odisha. Like many [[@architecture-temples|Hindu temples]], it faces east, so the first rays of the rising sun would reach the entrance.

Thousands of workers are thought to have worked on it for years. They used several kinds of stone, including a soft, greenish rock called chlorite for detailed carvings, and iron beams to hold some of the heavy blocks together.

What you see at Konark today is not the whole temple. The main shrine once had a towering spire, perhaps around 70 metres tall, which would have been visible far out at sea. European sailors called it the Black Pagoda and used it as a [[@lighthouses|landmark]].

That tower has fallen, and only its base remains. What still stands is the *jagamohana*, the great audience hall in front of it. By the early 1900s, it too was cracking. In 1903 British engineers filled it with sand and sealed its doors to stop it collapsing. In recent years, the Archaeological Survey of India has begun carefully removing that sand to repair the hall.

Nearly every surface at Konark is carved. You can see musicians, dancers, hunters, soldiers, elephants, kings, gods and scenes of everyday life, including people cooking, fighting and travelling. Some carvings show animals that were brought from far away, like a giraffe. Some historians think this shows that traders brought news, or even animals, from Africa.

Three large statues of Surya on the outer walls face different directions. Some people think they show the Sun at morning, noon and evening, linking again to time and the [[@seasons-why|seasons]].

sec.h: On a banknote and a heritage list
sec.t:
Konark became a [[@unesco-sites|UNESCO World Heritage Site]] in 1984. A picture of the temple appears on the back of India's ten-rupee note, and [[@wheel-invented|the wheel]] is one of Odisha's best-known symbols.

Every December, the Konark Dance Festival takes place in an open-air stage near the temple, with Odissi and other classical dancers performing. Many of the poses carved on the walls look like movements from Odissi dance, so it can feel as if the stone dancers have stepped down to join them.

text: A plucked string wobbles back and forth very fast. Each wobble pushes on the air, sending out waves of [[sound|sound]]. The number of wobbles each second is called the frequency, and your ear hears it as pitch. More wobbles mean a higher note.

A shorter string wobbles faster. When a sitar player presses a string against a fret, only the part between the fret and the bridge can vibrate. Press halfway along and that part is exactly half as long, so it vibrates twice as fast. You hear the same note, one [[octave|octave]] higher: Sa to the next Sa.
Length is one of three things that set a note. Tightness and thickness matter too.

quiz.prompt: A sitar player presses a string exactly halfway along its length and plucks it. What happens to the note?

options.t: It goes up by one octave
It goes down by one octave
It stays the same but gets louder

quiz.reveal: Half the string vibrates twice as fast as the whole string. Twice the vibrations sounds like the same note, only higher, from Sa to the next Sa. Musicians call that jump an octave.

src: Rossing T.D. (2014) Springer Handbook of Acoustics.

d.try: Hold a ruler flat on a table with most of it sticking out over the edge. Press the end on the table firmly and twang the free end. Now slide the ruler so less of it sticks out, and twang again. The shorter the part that wobbles, the faster it moves and the higher the buzz.
myth: High notes travel faster through the air than low notes.
All notes travel through air at the same speed, about 343 metres a second. If they didn't, music heard from far away would arrive with its high and low notes jumbled up.

sec.h: Three ways to change a note
sec.t:
Tighten a string and it springs back faster, so its pitch rises. That's what musicians do when they turn the pegs to tune up. A thicker, heavier string moves more slowly, so it plays lower. That's why the bass strings on a [[@guitar|guitar]] are fat and the high strings thin.

The same rules work in your body. Your vocal cords are stretched folds of tissue in your throat. Tighten them and your [[@voice|voice]] goes up. Children's vocal cords are shorter and lighter than adults', which is one reason children's voices are higher. A mosquito's [[@insect-flight|whine]] is high for a related reason: its tiny wings beat several hundred times a second.

A sitar has a long hollow neck and a round body, traditionally made from a dried gourd. Most have six or seven playing strings, plucked with a wire pick worn on the finger. Underneath lie eleven to thirteen thinner sympathetic strings. Nobody plucks them. They start to hum on their own when a matching note is played above, adding a shimmering echo.

The frets are curved metal bars tied to the neck, so the player can move them to suit a [[raga|raga]]. Players also pull a string sideways across a fret. That stretches it, raises its pitch and creates the sliding, singing notes, called *meend*, that make sitar music sound so much like a voice.

Play a sitar and you hear a bright, buzzing tone, quite unlike a guitar. The secret is the bridge, a wide, gently curved piece of bone or horn. The vibrating string brushes against it with every wobble, which adds many extra high tones. Shaping that curve just right is a skilled job called *jawari*.

In 1921, the physicist C. V. Raman, who later won the Nobel Prize, published a study of how Indian stringed instruments such as the [[@veena|veena]] and tanpura produce their rich sound. Decades later, [[@ravi-shankar|Ravi Shankar]] carried the sitar's sound to the West, playing at festivals in the USA in the 1960s. Behind every [[@raga-time|raga]] he played were the same simple rules about how strings move.

text: Environmental heroes are people who noticed something going wrong with nature and refused to look away. Some were scientists. Some were village women, farmers or a man with a bag of seedlings.

In the USA, John Muir campaigned to protect wild valleys, and Rachel Carson warned that [[pesticide|pesticides]] were poisoning birds. In India, [[@india-tree-mother|Saalumarada Thimmakka]] planted banyan trees along a road and Jadav Payeng grew a forest on a sandbar. The women of the [[@chipko|Chipko movement]] stood between loggers and their trees.
None of them had special powers. They had patience, and they kept going when others laughed.

sec.h: The man who grew a forest
sec.t:
In 1979, a teenager named Jadav Payeng saw snakes lying dead on a bare sandbar in the Brahmaputra river in Assam, killed by the heat after a flood. There was no shade anywhere.

He began planting [[@bamboo|bamboo]], then other trees, watering them by hand. He kept going for decades. Today that forest, called Molai after his nickname, covers hundreds of hectares. Deer, rhinos, tigers and elephants have been seen there. In 2015 he received the Padma Shri, one of India's highest awards. People call him the Forest Man of India.

In Karnataka, Saalumarada Thimmakka and her husband had no children. So they planted banyan saplings along the road between the villages of Hulikal and Kudur and cared for them like children, carrying water over long distances.

About 385 [[@banyan|banyan]] trees now line roughly 4 km of road. Her name, "Saalumarada", means "row of trees" in Kannada. She received the Padma Shri in 2019.

sec.h: The book that saved the eagles

sec.t:
A century earlier, the Scottish-American writer John Muir walked the Sierra Nevada mountains in California and wrote about them with joy. His articles helped make [[@yosemite|Yosemite]] a national park in 1890.

In India, Salim Ali spent his life watching birds. His *Book of Indian Birds* got generations of children looking up, and he helped save [[@wetlands|wetlands]] like Bharatpur in Rajasthan, now Keoladeo National Park.

You don't need a degree to help. Every February, thousands of people in India and the USA take part in the Great Backyard Bird Count, noting the birds they see for at least 15 minutes. Scientists use these counts to track which birds are thriving and which are disappearing.

In cities like Bengaluru, groups of neighbours have cleaned and revived dying lakes, removing rubbish and stopping sewage flowing in. In American towns, volunteers pick litter off beaches and riverbanks and record what they find, which helps show where plastic comes from.

Heroes like Payeng and Thimmakka started small, with one sapling. Lots of small efforts, added up, can change a landscape.

Young people have joined in too. In 2018, a Swedish schoolgirl named [[@greta-and-youth|Greta Thunberg]] sat outside her country's [[parliament|parliament]] every Friday to demand action on [[@climate-change|climate change]]. Millions of students around the world copied her school strike. Whether by protest, science or a spade, people keep finding their own way to help.

text: Great teachers explain things clearly, believe their students can do well and find out quickly what each child has understood. They ask good questions, give useful feedback and make a classroom feel safe enough that being wrong is fine.

Researchers have studied teaching for decades. The teachers who help students learn most are not always the most entertaining. They tend to break hard ideas into steps, check often for understanding, and go back over things at the right time. They also care, and their students can tell. Almost everyone can name a teacher who changed something for them, and it's usually for one of these reasons.

st.prompt: Scientists compared different ways of studying. Which one helps people remember the most?

options.t: Testing yourself, for example with flashcards
Reading your notes again and again
Highlighting the important parts

st.reveal: Pulling a fact out of your memory makes that memory stronger. Rereading and highlighting feel useful, but in experiments they help much less. That's why good teachers ask lots of questions, not just give lots of answers.

d.try: Teach someone at home something you learned this week, in five minutes, without notes. Then ask them to explain it back to you. You'll quickly find the parts you didn't understand yourself, which is exactly what teachers discover when they plan a lesson.
myth: Everyone has a learning style, visual, auditory or hands-on, and learns best when taught that way.

Many people have a preference, but careful studies have not found that teaching to a person's preferred style helps them learn more. What helps is matching the method to the subject, like using maps for geography and practice for music.

sec.t:
In 1887, Anne Sullivan arrived at a farmhouse in Alabama to teach Helen Keller, a six-year-old who could neither see nor hear. For weeks, Sullivan spelled words into Helen's hand with finger shapes. Helen copied them but didn't understand that they meant anything.

Then, at a water pump, Sullivan held one of Helen's hands under the cold stream and spelled w-a-t-e-r into the other. Helen later wrote that in that moment she understood that everything had a name. By evening she had learned 30 words. She grew up to graduate from college and write books. Sullivan had found the one thing that made it click, which great teachers keep looking for.

One thing scientists have found again and again is the testing effect. When you try to recall something from [[@memory|memory]], even if you struggle, you remember it better later. Good teachers use quick quizzes, questions in class and "explain it to your partner" moments, not to give marks, but to help memories stick.

Spacing helps too. Going back to a topic after a few days, then a few weeks, works better than one long session. And feedback matters most when it's specific. "Check the units in question 3" helps more than "good work" or "try harder".

A teacher in a class of 40 can't give each child an hour a day. Great teachers notice anyway. They see who has gone quiet, who is bored because it's too easy, and who is hiding confusion behind a smile.

Many children in India learn in a language that isn't the one they speak at home. Good teachers bridge that gap with stories, local examples and patience. In the US, teachers also work with children who are still learning English.

In 2020, Ranjitsinh Disale, a primary school teacher from Solapur in Maharashtra, won the Global Teacher Prize. He added [[@qr-codes|QR codes]] to textbooks so children could scan them and watch lessons and stories in their own language. He shared half his prize money with the other finalists.

Tools change, from slates to smartboards. The main ingredients don't. A teacher who knows the subject well, explains it clearly and cares whether you understand it is hard to beat.

Teaching isn't just the time in the classroom. Teachers plan lessons, mark work, meet parents and keep learning themselves. India had about 98 lakh school teachers in 2023 to 2024, one of the largest teaching workforces in the world.

India celebrates Teachers' Day on 5 September, the birthday of S. Radhakrishnan, a philosopher and teacher who became President. The rest of the world marks World Teachers' Day on 5 October. In the US, Teacher Appreciation Week comes in May, when many children bring a card or a flower.

text: A president and a prime minister can both lead a country, but they get their power in different ways. In a presidential system, like the United States, voters choose the president separately from the lawmakers, and the president is both head of state and head of the government.

In a parliamentary system, like India or Britain, voters elect a [[parliament|parliament]]. The leader of the majority there becomes prime minister and runs the government. A separate head of state, a [[monarch|monarch]] or a president, stays mostly above party politics.

sec.t:
In the United States, the President is elected for four years and can serve at most two terms. The President leads the government, commands the [[@military|armed forces]] and represents the country abroad. But the President is not a member of [[@congress-usa|Congress]] and cannot make laws alone.

A US President cannot be removed just because Congress dislikes their policies. The only way to remove one early is impeachment, a trial for serious wrongdoing, and no president has ever been removed that way.

India's President is elected for five years, but not by ordinary voters. An electoral college of MPs and members of state assemblies chooses them. The President signs bills into law, appoints the Prime Minister, and is supreme commander of the armed forces.

In practice the President acts on the advice of the Prime Minister and ministers. Still, the job carries weight. A President can send a bill back to Parliament once to be reconsidered, and decides who to invite to form a government when no party has a clear majority. The President's official home in [[@delhi|Delhi]], Rashtrapati Bhavan, was designed by Edwin Lutyens and has about 340 rooms. [[@white-house|The White House]] has 132.

Some countries use a bit of both. France has a powerful elected president and also a prime minister who needs parliament's support. Sometimes the two come from rival parties and have to share the work. The French call this "cohabitation", which means living together.

Other countries have a president with almost no political power at all. Germany's president, for example, signs laws and greets visiting leaders, while the chancellor, Germany's name for a prime minister, runs the government. The title alone does not tell you how much power someone has. You have to read the country's [[constitution|constitution]].

Political scientists disagree. A presidential system gives a clear leader for a fixed term, and it is hard to remove them early. A parliamentary system can replace a leader quickly, but governments may fall if the majority splits. Each country chose its system from its own history. India picked the British-style system it already knew when it wrote its Constitution, and every [[@democracy-what|democracy]] keeps arguing about how to make its own version work better.

text: An [[atom|atom]] is about a tenth of a billionth of a metre across, depending on the type. That size is so small that ordinary words stop working, so scientists use the nanometre, a billionth of a metre. Most atoms are between 0.1 and 0.5 nanometres wide.

To picture it, take a single human hair. It is very roughly a tenth of a millimetre thick. You could lay something like a million atoms side by side across it. A full stop at the end of this sentence could hold billions of billions of them.
Everything you can touch, from a cricket ball to your own skin, is built from atoms like these.

st.reveal: Almost all of an atom's mass is packed into its tiny nucleus at the centre. The electrons whizz around in a cloud far outside it. Everything in between is empty, which means you, your chair and the Earth are mostly empty space too.

sec.t:
The easiest way to travel down to an atom is in steps of ten.

Start with your hand, about 10 centimetres wide. Ten times smaller is a fingernail's width, about 1 centimetre. Ten times smaller again is a grain of sand, about a millimetre. Ten more is the width of a hair. Ten more is a single cell in your body. Keep going: a bacterium, then a virus, then a large [[molecule|molecule]], then a small one.

After about nine steps from your hand, you arrive at an atom. Each step divides the size by ten, so nine steps divide it by a thousand million. Scientists write this as 10⁻¹⁰ metres.

In 1977, the American designers Charles and Ray Eames made a short film called *Powers of Ten*. It zooms out from a picnic to the edge of the known universe, then back into a single atom, one step of ten at a time.

An atom has a tiny centre called a [[nucleus|nucleus]], made of [[proton|protons]] and neutrons. Around it, much further out, are even lighter particles called electrons.

The nucleus is about 100,000 times smaller across than the whole atom. If an atom were blown up to the size of a cricket stadium, its nucleus would be roughly a pea on the centre of the pitch. The [[electron|electrons]] would be somewhere out in the stands.

Yet almost all the atom's mass is in that pea. The rest is mostly empty space. You don't fall through your chair because the electrons in your atoms and the chair's atoms push each other away.

{{story:body-cells}}

For a long time, atoms were an idea. Around 2,400 years ago, the Greek thinker Democritus suggested that everything was made of tiny pieces that couldn't be cut, *atomos*. In India, the philosopher Kanada, of the Vaisheshika school, taught a similar idea of tiny eternal particles called *paramanu*.

Atoms are far too small to see with an ordinary [[microscope|microscope]], because they are smaller than the waves of light. Then, in 1981, two scientists at IBM in Zurich, Gerd Binnig and Heinrich Rohrer, built the scanning tunnelling microscope. It feels a surface with an extremely sharp tip and maps the bumps, one atom at a time. They won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1986.

In 1989, IBM scientist Don Eigler used one of these [[@microscopes|microscopes]] to move 35 single atoms of xenon into the letters "IBM".

Scientists use the same powers of ten to go upwards. Your body contains about 30 to 40 lakh crore [[@body-cells|cells]], each made of countless atoms. A strand of [[@dna|DNA]] is only about 2 nanometres wide but, stretched out, the DNA in one of your cells would be about 2 metres long.

Going up instead of down, the Earth is about 10⁷ metres across. Our [[@galaxies|galaxy]] is about 10²¹ metres. Somewhere in the middle of all those steps, at about one or two metres, is you.

text: Marco Polo was a merchant from [[@venice|Venice]] who travelled across Asia to [[@china-today|China]] in the 13th century. He lived there for about 17 years at the court of the [[@mongols|Mongol]] emperor Kublai Khan.

He saw huge, well-run cities, paper money, coal used as fuel, a postal service with relay stations and the busy port of Quanzhou, full of ships. On his way home by sea, he passed through Southeast Asia, [[@sri-lanka|Sri Lanka]] and the coasts of south and west India. Back in Europe, he described it all in a book that became one of the most famous travel books ever written. For centuries, it shaped what Europeans imagined about Asia, and it inspired later explorers, including [[@columbus|Columbus]].

st.reveal: He wrote that the stones burned like logs and kept a fire going all night. Coal was already widely used in China for heating and cooking. In much of Europe at the time, people mainly burned wood.

n.certNote: Most historians accept that Marco Polo went to China, because his book contains details few outsiders could have known. A few scholars have argued he may have relied on others' stories, partly because he never mentions tea or the Great Wall.

sec.t:
Marco's father Niccolò and uncle Maffeo were merchants who had already visited Kublai Khan. In 1271 they set out again, taking 17-year-old Marco with them.

They travelled overland along the [[@silk-road|Silk Road]], through Persia, across the high Pamir mountains and along the edge of the Gobi Desert. The journey took over three years. Kublai Khan welcomed them at his summer palace at Shangdu, which English poets later called Xanadu.

sec.h: Pearls, diamonds and a queen in India
sec.t:
In 1292, the Polos left by sea, escorting a Mongol princess to Persia. Their fleet stopped in Sumatra and Sri Lanka, then sailed along India's coast.

Marco described [[@pearls|pearl divers]] off the Tamil coast and a kingdom on the east coast, the [[@kakatiyas|Kakatiya kingdom]], which he said was ruled wisely by a queen. Historians identify her as Rudrama Devi, one of the few women rulers in Indian history. He also told a tall tale about how diamonds were collected from deep valleys by tricking eagles into carrying meat with diamonds stuck to it.

Marco reached home in 1295. A few years later he was captured in a war between Venice and its rival Genoa. In prison he met Rustichello da Pisa, a writer of romances, and told him his adventures.

Rustichello wrote them down, adding a few flourishes of his own. The book was copied by hand into many languages, and each copy changed a little. Italians nicknamed it *Il Milione*, perhaps because Marco described everything in millions.

Some readers have doubted Marco. His book never mentions tea, [[@food-chopsticks|chopsticks]] or the [[@great-wall|Great Wall]]. In 1995, historian Frances Wood argued he might have collected stories from Persian and Arab traders instead.

Most historians disagree. In 2013, Hans Ulrich Vogel showed that Marco's descriptions of Chinese paper money and salt production were detailed and accurate, matching Chinese records. A later story says that, on his deathbed in 1324, friends asked him to admit he'd made things up, and he replied that he had not told half of what he saw.

text: The Himalayas stretch about 2,400 km across Asia, from Pakistan in the west, through India, Nepal and [[@bhutan|Bhutan]], to Tibet in the east. Millions of people live among them, from villages in warm green valleys to high pastures far above the tree line.

They belong to many different peoples. There are Ladakhis and Kashmiris in the west, [[@people-shepherds-himalaya|Gaddi shepherds]] in Himachal Pradesh, and Garhwalis and Kumaonis in [[@uttarakhand|Uttarakhand]]. Nepal is home to [[@people-sherpas|Sherpas]], Gurungs, Tamangs and many others. Further east live the Lepchas and Bhutias of [[@sikkim|Sikkim]], the people of Bhutan and the Monpa of Arunachal Pradesh, with Tibetans on the high plateau to the north. They speak dozens of languages and follow Hindu, Buddhist, Muslim and older local traditions.

st.prompt: Why do many Sherpas and Tibetans cope better with thin mountain air than visitors from the plains?

options.t: Their bodies have adapted over many generations
They train by holding their breath
They secretly carry oxygen tanks

st.reveal: People whose ancestors have lived high up for thousands of years tend to have bodies that use oxygen more efficiently. Part of this is in their genes, passed down through families.

Sherpa is the name of a people, an ethnic group from eastern Nepal. Many Sherpas work on mountains, but many do other jobs, and many mountain workers come from other communities.

sec.t:
At 4,000 m, each breath holds only about 60% of the oxygen it would at sea level. Newcomers get headaches and feel breathless. People whose families have lived high up for thousands of years often cope much better.

Tibetans, for example, tend to breathe faster and have bodies that use oxygen in a slightly different way. In 2014 scientists reported that many Tibetans carry a version of a [[gene|gene]] called EPAS1 that seems to help. Surprisingly, it appears to have come from the Denisovans, an ancient group of humans whose DNA survives in some living people. Sherpas, who descend from Tibetan migrants, share some of these advantages.

For many people, the mountains are sacred. Hindu pilgrims travel to Kedarnath, Badrinath and Amarnath. Buddhists build [[monastery|monasteries]] on ridges, such as Hemis in [[@ladakh|Ladakh]] and Tawang in Arunachal Pradesh, the largest monastery in India. Colourful prayer flags flutter on passes, printed with prayers that, by tradition, the wind carries away.

People have protected their mountains, too. In 1973, villagers in what is now Uttarakhand began hugging trees to stop them being cut down. Women such as Gaura Devi of Reni village led the way, and the [[@chipko|Chipko movement]] became famous across the world.

The Sherpa people of Nepal's Khumbu region became famous through [[@mountaineering|mountaineering]]. Tenzing Norgay, a Sherpa, reached the top of Everest with Edmund Hillary of New Zealand in 1953, as told in [[@everest-first|the first Everest climb]].

Today many Sherpas work as climbing guides and high-altitude workers, a dangerous and skilled job. Some of the most experienced have climbed Everest more than twenty times. The mountains themselves are still growing by a few millimetres a year, because India keeps pushing into Asia, as explained in [[@himalaya-form|how the Himalayas formed]].

text: Puducherry feels French because it was ruled by France for most of the time between 1674 and 1954, much longer than the British ruled most of India. The French laid out its old town, built its churches and government buildings, and left behind their language, food and even street signs.

Walk through the old seaside quarter and you see mustard-yellow villas with white shutters, bougainvillea over the gates, and street names like Rue Romain Rolland. Policemen wear red caps called kepis, a French style. A French school, a French consulate and bakeries selling croissants sit a few streets from Tamil temples.
It became part of India in 1954, seven years after independence, and its name changed from Pondicherry to Puducherry in 2006.

sec.t:
Puducherry is not one block of land. It is four separate pieces. Puducherry town and Karaikal sit inside Tamil Nadu. Mahe is on the Kerala coast, on the other side of India. Yanam is in Andhra Pradesh, more than 600 km from Puducherry town.

Each was a French trading post, and they stayed together after 1954. Mahe and Yanam are small [[enclave|enclaves]], surrounded by other states. That's why Puducherry's government uses five languages: Tamil, Malayalam and Telugu for its three regions, plus English and French.

When France handed over Puducherry, people living there were given a choice. They could become Indian citizens or keep French citizenship. Several thousand chose France. Their families still live in Puducherry today, carrying French passports.

So during French presidential elections, polling booths open in Puducherry, and voters line up in a small Indian town to elect the leader of a country more than 7,000 km away. Some French-Tamil families have relatives in Paris, Lyon and Marseille. Many older people in the town still speak French at home.

The old French quarter is built in a tidy grid, a plan that was unusual for Indian towns at the time. A canal once divided it into a European quarter by the sea and a Tamil quarter inland. The canal is still there, though the old names have faded.

Along the seafront, the long Promenade Beach is closed to traffic every evening, and families walk along it as the sea breeze comes in. Near it stands a statue of Joan of Arc, the French heroine, and a war memorial to soldiers from Puducherry who fought for France in the First World War.

Just north of the town, Auroville, a township founded in 1968, brings together people from dozens of countries. Puducherry is not the only place in India that feels European. Down the west coast, [[@goa|Goa]] was ruled by Portugal until 1961, even longer, and its churches, food and words still show it. And not far north lies [[@chennai|Chennai]], which began as a British fort only a few decades before the French arrived here.

text: Karnataka is a large state in southern India, stretching from the Arabian Sea coast across the forested Western Ghats to a dry, rocky plateau. Its capital, [[@bengaluru|Bengaluru]], is famous as India's technology hub. But the state is also known for its history, its coffee, its silk and sandalwood, and the Kannada language.

It holds the ruins of Hampi, once the capital of a great [[empire|empire]], the palaces of Mysuru, and ancient Jain and Hindu temples. Its hills grow most of India's coffee, and its forests shelter elephants and tigers. People speak Kannada across the state, and Tulu, Konkani and Kodava are spoken in some regions too.

st.reveal: The story says that in the 1600s, Baba Budan hid seven beans in his clothes on the way back from pilgrimage and planted them in the Chandragiri hills. Historians can't confirm the details, but the hills now carry his name, Baba Budangiri.

sec.h: A giant carved from one rock
sec.t:
At Shravanabelagola, a small town in Karnataka, a statue of Gommateshwara, also called Bahubali, stands on top of a hill. It is carved from a single block of [[granite|granite]] and is about 17 m tall, taller than a five-storey building. It was made around 983 CE and is one of the most important places for Jains.

According to Jain tradition, Bahubali stood in meditation so long that vines grew up his legs, and the statue shows them climbing around him. Every 12 years or so, a huge ceremony called the Mahamastakabhisheka takes place. Priests on scaffolding pour milk, turmeric and flower petals over the statue's head.

The legend goes that in the 1600s, a Sufi saint named Baba Budan smuggled seven coffee beans from Yemen and planted them in the hills near Chikkamagaluru. Whatever the true details, Karnataka now grows about 70% of India's [[@coffee|coffee]]. Plantations in Kodagu (also called Coorg) and Chikkamagaluru grow coffee in the shade of taller trees, alongside pepper vines and cardamom.

These hills are part of the [[@western-ghats|Western Ghats]], a mountain range that catches heavy [[monsoon|monsoon]] rain. Jog Falls, where the Sharavati river plunges about 253 m, roars in the rainy season. The forests are home to many [[species|species]] found nowhere else.

Mysore silk, woven in shining colours with gold borders, is famous across India. So is Karnataka's sandalwood, whose fragrant oil goes into soaps and incense. [[@mysore-palace|Mysuru's palace]] and its Dasara festival draw huge crowds each year. Wooden toys from the town of [[@channapatna-toys|Channapatna]], painted with bright natural colours, are another Karnataka speciality.

On the coast, people perform Yakshagana, an all-night theatre of dance, drumming and song, with huge headdresses and bright face paint. The Kannada language has a written history stretching back well over a thousand years, and Kannada writers have won the Jnanpith, India's top literary prize, eight times. That's more than writers in most other Indian languages, a fact many in Karnataka are proud of.

text: Pune is a big city in Maharashtra, about 150 km by road south-east of [[@mumbai|Mumbai]], on a plateau at the edge of the Western Ghats. It was once the seat of the Peshwas, who ran the Maratha Empire, and later became a centre of Indian reform and the freedom struggle.

Today it's known for its many colleges, which earned it the nickname "Oxford of the East", and for its car and motorcycle factories and software companies. It's also known for a pleasant [[climate|climate]], its public [[@tilak|Ganeshotsav]], and street snacks like misal pav. Its old name, Poona, was officially changed to Pune in 1978.

For a long time, it was mostly a family festival at home. In 1893, Bal Gangadhar Tilak helped turn it into a large public celebration in Pune, partly so that people could gather together at a time when British rules limited political meetings.

sec.t:
[[@shivaji|Shivaji]], founder of the Maratha kingdom, spent much of his childhood in Pune in the 1630s and 1640s. A century later, the Peshwas, the chief ministers of the Maratha rulers, made Pune their capital. From here they controlled a large part of India.

In 1732, Peshwa Bajirao I completed a grand fortified palace called Shaniwar Wada. Most of it burned down in 1828, but its massive walls and gates still stand. One gate is studded with long iron spikes to stop elephants charging it. In 1818, the British defeated the Marathas, and Pune became an important British army base.

Ganesh Chaturthi was long celebrated mostly at home. In 1893, the freedom fighter Bal Gangadhar Tilak helped turn it into a huge public festival, with community pandals, music and speeches. British rules made political meetings difficult. A religious festival brought large crowds together, and ideas spread among them.

Pune's link to the freedom struggle continued. During the [[@quit-india|Quit India]] movement in 1942, the British held Mahatma Gandhi and his wife Kasturba in the Aga Khan Palace in Pune. Kasturba died there in 1944, and her memorial stands in its gardens. Gandhi's secretary, Mahadev Desai, also died there during the same imprisonment, in 1942.

Pune has dozens of colleges and research institutes. The Film and Television Institute of India trains actors, directors and camera operators, and many famous film people studied there. The National Defence Academy, where young officers train for the army, navy and air force, is just outside the city.

The city is also a major centre for making cars, motorcycles and machines, and later grew into a hub for software companies. Scientists at the Giant Metrewave Radio Telescope, about 80 km away, use 30 huge dish antennas, each 45 m across, to listen to radio waves from distant [[galaxy|galaxies]]. On weekends, many people head out of the city to the forts and green hills of the [[@western-ghats|Western Ghats]], climbing paths once used by Maratha soldiers.

text: Anne Frank was a Jewish girl who hid from the Nazis in [[@amsterdam|Amsterdam]] during the [[@world-war-two|Second World War]]. For just over two years she kept a [[@diaries|diary]] in a secret set of rooms behind her father's office. She was found, arrested and sent to concentration camps, where she died at 15.

Her diary survived. It was published in 1947 and has been read by tens of millions of people. It matters because it lets readers meet one real, funny, moody, clever teenager among the millions of people killed in the [[holocaust|Holocaust]].

st.prompt: Who saved Anne's diary after the people in hiding were arrested?

options.t: Miep Gies, one of the helpers who brought them food

A police officer who handed it to a museum

st.reveal: After the arrest, Miep Gies collected Anne's papers from the floor of the hiding place and locked them away unread. When Anne's father Otto came back alone after the war, she gave them to him.

d.try: Keep a diary for one week. Each day, write about one small thing that happened and one thing you thought about it. At the end of the week, read it back and notice which entries show what you were really like.
myth: Anne wrote her diary only for herself and never meant anyone to read it.
In 1944 she heard a radio broadcast asking Dutch people to keep diaries and letters for after the war. She began rewriting her diary as a book, with a planned title, The Secret Annex.

sec.t:
For her 13th birthday on 12 June 1942, Anne was given an autograph book with a red-and-white checked cover. She decided to use it as a diary and wrote her entries as [[@letters-writing|letters]] to an imaginary friend, Kitty.

Less than a month later, her older sister Margot was ordered to report to a Nazi work camp. The family went into hiding the next day. Anne, Margot and their parents Otto and Edith were joined by four more people, packed into a few rooms at Prinsengracht 263.

On 4 August 1944 the police raided the annex. Nobody knows for certain who told them. All eight were sent to camps. Anne and Margot died of disease at Bergen-Belsen in [[@germany|Germany]] in early 1945, only weeks before the camp was freed. Otto was the only one of the eight to survive.

When he read the diary, he found a daughter he felt he had never fully known. He decided to fulfil her wish to be published.

sec.h: Why so many people read it
sec.t:
History books give numbers: about six million Jewish people were murdered. A number that large is hard to feel. Anne's diary gives one name, one voice and one ordinary bedroom wall covered in film-star pictures.

It has been put into more than 70 languages through [[@translation|translation]] and is read in schools across India, the United States and Europe. It has been made into plays and films. The first edition left out some passages, such as Anne's sharpest words about her mother. Later editions put them back, so readers now meet a fuller and more honest Anne. People have come to see the parallels with children forced from their homes today, including [[@refugees|refugees]] fleeing war.

The annex opened as the Anne Frank House museum in 1960. The rooms are kept empty, as Otto asked, and the original diary is on display. In 2009 UNESCO added Anne's diaries to its Memory of the World register, a list of documents that belong to everyone. Like [[@malala|Malala]] decades later, Anne showed that a young person's words, written down, can reach the whole world.

text: Ganesha, the elephant-headed god, is one of the best-loved figures in Hindu stories. He is the remover of obstacles and the god people pray to before starting anything new, from a school exam to a wedding. He is also clever, kind and fond of sweets, especially the steamed dumplings called modak.

Children grow up with his stories. They learn how he got his elephant head and how he won a race around the world without leaving home. They hear why he has a broken tusk, and why he once cursed the Moon. They appear in temple carvings, comic books, cartoons and grandparents' bedtime tales, and get told loudest during [[@ganesh-chaturthi|Ganesh Chaturthi]].

st.prompt: In the famous race around the world, how did Ganesha beat his brother Kartikeya?

options.t: He walked around his parents, saying they were his whole world
He rode his mouse faster than a peacock
He took a shortcut through a tunnel

st.reveal: Kartikeya flew off around the world on his peacock. Ganesha calmly walked three times around Shiva and Parvati and said his parents were his world. In many tellings, he wins the prize, a magical fruit.

Different Puranas, the old story collections, give different versions. In the best-known one, Shiva cuts off the boy's head and replaces it with an elephant's. In another, the god Shani's gaze causes the loss. Different regions keep different tellings.

sec.t:
In the best-known version, the goddess Parvati made a boy from turmeric paste and brought him to life. She told him to guard the door while she bathed and let no one in.

When Shiva, her husband, came home, the boy blocked his way. They fought, and Shiva cut off the boy's head. Parvati was heartbroken and furious. To calm her, Shiva sent his followers to bring the head of the first creature they found. They returned with an elephant's head, and Shiva brought the boy back to life as Ganesha, making him leader of his followers.

Other Puranas tell it differently. In one, the planet god Shani glances at the baby and the head is lost. Indians have kept several versions side by side for centuries.

Ganesha is usually shown with one tusk broken. One story explains it this way. The sage Vyasa wanted to dictate the [[@mahabharata|Mahabharata]], the longest poem in the world, and asked Ganesha to write it down. Ganesha agreed on one condition: Vyasa must never stop. Vyasa added his own condition: Ganesha must understand every verse before writing it.

As they raced along, Ganesha's pen broke. Rather than stop, he snapped off his own tusk and kept writing with it. Other stories say he lost the tusk in a fight, but the writing story is the favourite of students.

sec.h: Why not to look at the Moon
sec.t:
One night, after a big feast of modaks, Ganesha was riding his mouse home with a full belly. The mouse tripped over a snake, Ganesha tumbled, and his belly burst open with sweets everywhere. The Moon, watching, laughed.

Angry, Ganesha cursed the Moon to fade away. The Moon begged forgiveness, so Ganesha softened the curse: it would shrink and grow each month. Some people say this is why the [[@moon-phases|Moon has phases]]. It's also why, in many homes, people avoid looking at the Moon on the night of Ganesh Chaturthi.

In 1893, the freedom fighter [[@tilak|Bal Gangadhar Tilak]] helped turn Ganesh Chaturthi in Pune from a family festival into a huge public one, bringing people together. Today giant idols fill Mumbai's streets. Ganesha is honoured in Nepal, Thailand, Indonesia and even Japan, where a form of him is called Kangiten.

He is a god who likes sweets, rides a mouse and wins with brains, not muscle. His neighbour in many temples is the strong and loyal [[@myths-hanuman|Hanuman]].

text: Tinkle is an Indian comics magazine that started in November 1980. It was founded by Anant Pai, a chemical engineer turned publisher whom readers knew as Uncle Pai, at India Book House in Bombay. He had already created *Amar Chitra Katha*, the comics that retell Indian myths and history.

Tinkle was meant to be lighter and more playful. Each issue mixed funny comic strips, folk tales, puzzles, quizzes and short science facts. It soon became one of the most popular [[@childrens-magazines|children's magazines]] in India, and characters like Suppandi and Shikari Shambu became household names. Many parents who read it as children now buy it for their own kids.

st.reveal: Anant Pai began Amar Chitra Katha in 1967 to retell Indian myths, legends and history as comics. Thirteen years later he started Tinkle, which was lighter, funnier and full of readers' own contributions.

sec.h: Uncle Pai and a quiz show
sec.t:
Anant Pai often told how [[@amar-chitra-katha|Amar Chitra Katha]] began. In 1967 he saw a quiz on television in which Indian children could answer questions about Greek myths but not about the [[@ramayana|Ramayana]]. He felt children were losing touch with their own stories. Pai already knew comics well. Born in 1929 in Karkala, in Karnataka, he had worked at The Times of India, where he was involved with Indrajal Comics, which brought the American hero the Phantom to Indian readers.

Comics, he decided, were the answer. *Amar Chitra Katha* became a huge success. By the late 1970s, Pai wanted a magazine that would do more than retell old legends. He wanted something that was funny, that taught a little science and that let children take part.

So in 1980, *Tinkle* was born. Pai signed his messages to readers as Uncle Pai, the name generations of children came to know him by.

{{story:comics-art}}

Tinkle's most famous character is Suppandi, a simple, good-hearted village boy who keeps getting new jobs and keeps losing them. Tell him to "keep an eye on the milk" and he will stare at it as it boils over. The early Suppandi stories grew out of folk tales sent in by readers and were drawn by the artist Ram Waeerkar.

Shikari Shambu is a "great hunter" who is actually terrified of animals and succeeds only by accident. Kalia is a clever crow who protects smaller animals from Chamataka the jackal and Doob Doob the crocodile. Real [[@crow-smart|crows]] are among the cleverest birds, so Kalia fits right in. Tantri the Mantri is a minister who keeps plotting to seize the throne and always fails.

Tinkle's big idea was that readers could join in. Children sent jokes, stories and facts, and the best were printed with their names. Seeing your name in a national magazine was a thrill many readers still remember.

Each issue also had puzzles, "Tell me why" style science questions and stories from across [[@india-states-tour|India's regions]]. Tinkle came out in English and, at various times, in other Indian languages too.

Over the years, Tinkle launched thicker "digests" that collected old favourites, and holiday specials packed with extra stories. India Book House's comics later became part of a company called Amar Chitra Katha Pvt Ltd, which publishes Tinkle today.

Characters like Suppandi have appeared in animated shows and online. Anant Pai died in 2011, but his magazine kept going. Along with [[@comics-india|Indian comics]] such as *Chacha Chaudhary* and later TV heroes like [[@chhota-bheem|Chhota Bheem]], Tinkle showed that Indian children wanted funny stories set in places that looked like home.

text: Ice cream is made by freezing a mixture of milk, cream and sugar while stirring it all the time. The stirring, called churning, does two jobs. It keeps the ice crystals tiny, so the ice cream feels smooth on your tongue instead of icy. It also whips in air, which makes it soft and light.

In a factory, the mixture is first heated to kill germs, then mixed so the fat is spread evenly. It is cooled, flavoured and churned in a freezer that pumps in air. Finally it is hardened at very low temperature. A good ice cream is a careful balance of [[crystal|ice crystals]], fat, sugar syrup and air.

st.prompt: In old ice cream makers, the tub of cream sat in a bucket of ice. Why did people add salt to the ice?

options.t: Salt makes the ice melt at a lower temperature, so the mixture gets colder
Salt keeps the ice from melting at all
Salt flavours the ice cream

st.reveal: Salt dissolves in the thin film of water on the ice and lowers its freezing point. The ice melts, and melting pulls heat from everything around it, including the cream. The salty slush can drop well below 0°C.

myth: Eating ice cream gives you a cold.
Colds are caused by viruses, not by cold food. Ice cream can feel uncomfortable on a sore throat, and a sudden "brain freeze" is real, but neither causes infection.

sec.t:
Sugar does more than sweeten. It lowers the freezing point of water, so not all the water turns to ice. A little stays as thick, sweet syrup, which keeps ice cream soft enough to scoop.

Fat coats the tiny ice crystals and air bubbles and keeps them from joining up. That's why ice cream made with cream feels richer than ice made from fruit juice.

Kulfi is made differently. Milk is boiled slowly for a long time until much of its water evaporates and it thickens. Sugar, [[@cardamom-pepper|cardamom]], pistachios or [[@saffron|saffron]] are added. Then it is poured into cone-shaped moulds and frozen without churning.

With little air and less water, kulfi is dense and creamy, and melts slowly even on a hot afternoon. It is often linked with the [[@mughals|Mughal]] court. Records from [[@akbar|Akbar]]'s time describe ice and snow brought down from the mountains to cool drinks in the royal kitchen. Kulfi sellers, called kulfiwalas, still [[@food-trucks|push carts]] with clay pots packed with ice and salt, the old trick at work.

Ice cream became a luxury treat in the young United States. Records show that [[@george-washington|George Washington]] spent about 200 dollars on ice cream in one summer in 1790, a large sum then. Ice cream was made with ice cut from frozen lakes in winter and stored in icehouses.

By the 1900s, factories and home fridges made it cheap. Ice cream cones became popular at the 1904 World's Fair in St. Louis.

Eating ice cream too fast can cause a sudden, sharp headache, often called [[@body-brain-freeze|brain freeze]]. Scientists think the cold on the roof of your mouth makes blood vessels nearby narrow and then widen quickly, which nerves sense as pain.

It goes away in less than a minute. Pressing your tongue against the roof of your mouth can help warm it up. Eating more slowly prevents it, and it gives you more time to enjoy the ice cream.
